title: Flexbox
summary: Flexbox is the one-dimensional layout model built for distributing space along a single axis. Learn the axis model, the grow/shrink/basis math, and the shrink bug that trips up almost everyone.

slides.markdown:
Before flexbox, centering something vertically was a running joke in front-end interviews — you reached for table layouts, negative margins, or `position: absolute` with a magic offset. Flexbox exists to fix exactly that class of problem: **distributing space along one axis** between a container and its children.

It is not a general-purpose layout system — that's [CSS Grid](css-grid)'s job for two dimensions. Flexbox shines at rows and columns of things that need to grow, shrink, or align against each other: navbars, toolbars, card rows, form controls, anything that reads as a single line or a single stack.

The skill isn't memorizing property names. It's understanding the **main axis vs cross axis** model well enough to know which property controls which axis without guessing.

slides.subTitle: Container, items, two axes
slides.markdown:
Set `display: flex` on a container and two things happen at once: the container becomes a **flex container**, and every direct child becomes a **flex item** — no matter what it was before (a `<div>`, a `<span>`, an `<li>`).

Every flex container has two axes, and which one is which depends on `flex-direction`:

- **Main axis** — the direction items are laid out along. `row` (the default) makes it horizontal; `column` makes it vertical.
- **Cross axis** — perpendicular to the main axis.

This is the single most important mental model in flexbox: **the property you reach for depends on which axis you mean**, not on "horizontal" or "vertical" literally. Switch `flex-direction` to `column` and every "horizontal" property now acts vertically. Candidates who memorize "justify-content = horizontal" get tripped the moment a column layout shows up.

slides.subTitle: Which axis, which property
slides.markdown:
Three alignment properties, each pinned to a specific axis:

| Property | Axis it controls | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `justify-content` | main axis | spaces/aligns items along the line they flow on |
| `align-items` | cross axis | aligns items *within* a single line |
| `align-content` | cross axis | spaces multiple *lines* apart (only matters with `flex-wrap: wrap` and extra cross-axis room) |

The `align-items` vs `align-content` confusion is the most common one in interviews: `align-items` moves individual items inside their line; `align-content` moves whole lines relative to each other. With a single line of items (the default, no wrap), `align-content` has nothing to do — there's only one line — which is why it silently "doesn't work" for people testing it on a simple row.

`justify-content: space-between` and `space-around` are the two values worth knowing cold: `space-between` pins the first and last items to the edges with equal gaps between the rest; `space-around` gives every item equal space on both sides, which visually halves the gap at the edges.

slides.subTitle: grow, shrink, basis
slides.markdown:
Three properties, usually written as the shorthand `flex: <grow> <shrink> <basis>`, decide how items react when the container has extra or missing space:

- **`flex-basis`** — the item's starting size *before* growing/shrinking is applied. Defaults to `auto` (use the item's `width`/`height`, or its content size).
- **`flex-grow`** — a unitless number that says how much of the *extra* space (beyond the basis) this item should absorb, relative to its siblings. `flex-grow: 2` takes twice the extra space of a sibling with `flex-grow: 1`. `0` (the default) means don't grow at all.
- **`flex-shrink`** — the mirror image for a container that's *too small*: how much of the overflow this item gives up, relative to siblings. Default is `1`, meaning items shrink by default.

`flex: 1` is shorthand for `flex: 1 1 0%` — grow, shrink, and start every item's basis at zero so all extra space is distributed purely by the grow ratio. That's why `flex: 1` on every child of a row makes them perfectly equal width regardless of content.

slides.sectionTitle: Seeing grow and shrink in action
slides.markdown:
Picture a 600px-wide flex container holding three items with basis 100px each — 300px used, 300px extra.

- If all three have `flex-grow: 1`, the extra 300px splits evenly: each item ends at 200px wide.
- If one has `flex-grow: 2` and the other two have `flex-grow: 1`, the extra splits 2:1:1 — the ratio, not a fixed amount — so the doubled item gets 150px of the extra and the others get 75px each, ending at 250px/175px/175px.

Now shrink the container to 240px, 60px under the 300px basis total. With every item at the default `flex-shrink: 1`, the 60px deficit divides evenly (roughly 20px off each, adjusted by each item's basis), so no single item is crushed disproportionately unless you've set a different shrink value or a `min-width` that resists it.

slides.subTitle: min-width: auto

slides.markdown:
By default a flex row never wraps — items shrink to fit, potentially past readability, rather than dropping to a new line. `flex-wrap: wrap` opts into multi-line behavior, turning the container into a set of lines that `align-content` can then space apart.

`gap` (not the older margin-hack approach) puts space *between* items without adding space at the container's outer edges — the same property Grid uses, which is why it's worth learning once. Before `gap` existed on flex containers, developers used `margin-right` on every item except the last, which meant fragile `:last-child` overrides. `gap: 16px` replaces all of that with one declaration that also survives wrapping correctly — a wrapped row still only gets gaps *between* items, on both axes.

slides.sectionTitle: When to reach for grid instead
slides.markdown:
Flexbox is one-dimensional by design: it optimizes one axis at a time, and its cross-axis alignment doesn't track across multiple lines the way a true grid does — a wrapped flex row's second line doesn't know what column widths the first line settled on.

Reach for [CSS Grid](css-grid) instead once you need to align content in **both directions simultaneously** — a dashboard with cards that must line up in columns *and* rows, or a page layout with a header, sidebar, and footer all related to each other spatially. Reach for flexbox when the layout is fundamentally a line: a toolbar, a tag list, a form's button row, anything you'd describe as "one row" or "one column" even if it wraps.

Many real UIs use both: Grid for the page skeleton, flexbox for the components living inside each grid cell. Knowing which one solves which problem — rather than defaulting to whichever you learned first — is the actual skill being tested when someone asks "flexbox or grid?"
